item.text:
## Permissive research handoff — Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil, 2022

The eight selected chapters were researched sequentially. No scores, score ranges, rankings, or judge-directed advice were produced.

The repository remains read-only because the shell sandbox failed at startup (`RTM_NEWADDR`), so I could not persist changes to `research-ledger-manifest.json`. The manifest delta is included below for parent persistence.

### Chapter 1B — Nuclear/existential risk

New evidence:

- `WEB053`: Brazil’s government described the PROSUB nuclear-powered submarine as an active strategic Armed Forces program, intended to strengthen maritime sovereignty and eventually transfer the vessel to Naval Operations Command. The 2022 government page does not establish a Bolsonaro-specific command decision, nuclear threat, or near-use episode. [Brazilian government program description](https://www.gov.br/en/government-of-brazil/latest-news/2022/brazil-is-developing-nuclear-powered-submarine), lines 62–72.  
  Mappings: `1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.3, 1B.4, 1B.5, 1B.6, 1B.7, 1B.8, 1B.9, 1B.10`

Targeted searches covered Brazil’s nuclear submarine, command transfer, nuclear safeguards, proliferation, threats, and catastrophic-risk events. No ruler-specific adverse episode or presidential nuclear command change was recovered.

Shortfall remains substantial: the evidence establishes institutional exposure and formal program continuity, not personal Bolsonaro responsibility.

### Chapter 2B — International peace/lawful security

New evidence:

- `WEB054`: Brazil’s Foreign Ministry publicly defended the administration’s Ukraine position after Bolsonaro’s Russia visit, stating that Brazil’s positions were clear, public, and repeatedly conveyed to partner governments and the UN Security Council. This is a primary official clarification and should be distinguished from Bolsonaro’s personal public messaging. [Brazilian Foreign Ministry statement](https://www.gov.br/mre/pt-br/canais_atendimento/imprensa/notas-a-imprensa/declaracoes-a-respeito-da-politica-externa-brasileira), lines 334–342.  
  Mappings: `2B.1, 2B.3, 2B.4, 2B.6, 2B.7, 2B.10`

Contrary searches covered arms transfers, proxy activity, external combat operations, civilian harm, sanctions, and peace initiatives. No defensible target-period evidence of Brazilian proxy warfare, external combat operations, or arms transfers to the Ukraine conflict was located.

The chapter is improved on official diplomatic posture but remains narrow. The Moscow visit should not represent Brazil’s entire international-security conduct.

### Chapter 3B — Domestic safety/protection

New evidence:

- `WEB055`: The Brazilian Health Ministry states that health assistance to the Yanomami deteriorated sharply between 2019 and 2022, producing underreporting of illness and deaths and compromising Indigenous rights. This is a later official retrospective statement; attribution is institutional and tenure-based, not proof of a personal order. [Brazilian Health Ministry FAQ](https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/missao-yanomami/faq/faq/o-ministerio-da-saude-esconde), lines 297–303.  
  Mappings: `3B.4, 3B.5, 3B.6, 3B.9, 3B.10`

Searches also covered federal remedies, protest policing, surveillance, due process, and complaint channels. No sufficiently precise federal corrective-action or surveillance-oversight record was recovered.

The chapter gains one official retrospective institutional unit, but personal attribution for individual violence and remedy effectiveness remains unresolved.

### Chapter 4B — Political freedom/authoritarian rule

No additional final evidence was added after contrary searches of election administration, electoral disinformation, public-resource use, campaign finance, court capture, surveillance, and opposition rights.

The existing TSE/OAS material remains the strongest balance: Bolsonaro’s attacks and delegitimization are documented, while election administration remained auditable and institutionally resilient. Later TSE proceedings were not upgraded where only a search-result summary or an intermediate judicial vote was accessible.

### Chapter 5B — Economic wellbeing

New evidence:

- `WEB056`: A TCU audit found that Auxílio Brasil could have involved more than R$2 billion in monthly irregular payments because of improper beneficiary inclusion; the program design encouraged inaccurate family-composition declarations and reduced cost-effectiveness compared with Bolsa Família. [TCU Auxílio Brasil audit](https://portal.tcu.gov.br/imprensa/noticias/auditoria-no-auxilio-brasil-constata-desvio-do-publico-alvo-do-programa), lines 6–24.  
  Mappings: `5B.1, 5B.3, 5B.5, 5B.7, 5B.8, 5B.9, 5B.10`

- `WEB057`: TCU’s review of Bolsonaro’s 2022 accounts found one irregularity, three improprieties, ten accounting distortions, insufficient fiscal information, and problems involving tax-benefit measures. The court nevertheless concluded that the totality of the examined management was not compromised. [TCU 2022 accounts review](https://portal.tcu.gov.br/imprensa/noticias/tcu-aprova-com-ressalvas-as-contas-de-2022-do-ex-presidente-da-republica), lines 40–56, 61–77.  
  Mappings: `5B.3, 5B.5, 5B.6, 5B.8, 5B.9, 5B.10, 8B.3, 8B.5, 8B.9`

- `WEB058`: The same TCU review identified substantial regional disparity in social tax benefits: 2022 per-capita benefits were much lower in the North and Northeast than in the Southeast. This is a distributional outcome, not proof of Bolsonaro’s personal intent. [TCU regional-benefit findings](https://portal.tcu.gov.br/imprensa/noticias/tcu-aprova-com-ressalvas-as-contas-de-2022-do-ex-presidente-da-republica), lines 83–88.  
  Mappings: `5B.7, 5B.8, 5B.10`

Targeted searches covered appointments, competition policy, productivity, anti-corruption, fiscal management, and regional distribution. Evidence remains strongest for transfer implementation and fiscal/distributional weaknesses; appointment competence and productivity policy remain thin.

### Chapter 6B — Social wellbeing

New evidence:

- `WEB059`: A UNICEF/Ipec survey published in September 2022 covered adolescents aged 11–19 across all Brazilian regions and examined school exclusion, learning recovery, and student mental health. [UNICEF 2022 education study](https://www.unicef.org/brazil/relatorios/educacao-brasileira-em-2022-a-voz-de-adolescentes), lines 59–82.  
  Mappings: `6B.2, 6B.4, 6B.5, 6B.8, 6B.10`

- `WEB060`: A UNICEF-supported survey of 3,245 municipalities found learning recovery was a major post-pandemic challenge; more than 85% of surveyed municipalities were working on learning-gap strategies, while transport, school meals, connectivity, and family participation constrained implementation. [UNICEF/Undime learning-recovery survey](https://www.unicef.org/brazil/comunicados-de-imprensa/recuperacao-da-aprendizagem-prioridade-e-desafio-para-maioria-das-redes-municipais-de-educacao), lines 58–84.  
  Mappings: `6B.2, 6B.4, 6B.5, 6B.6, 6B.8, 6B.10, 8B.7, 8B.10`

The searches attempted education recovery, school attendance, service quality, sanitation, housing, health management, and political conditionality. No adequate federal housing or broad service-quality evaluation was recovered. Federal/state/municipal responsibility remains an important attribution limit.

### Chapter 7B — Personal integrity/honesty

No new final evidence was added.

Targeted searches covered asset declarations, procurement benefit, appointments, family-network benefit, obstruction, correction behavior, vaccination records, and electoral statements. Later police accusations and investigative reporting were retained only as discovery or retrospective material where they lacked a settled target-period adjudication.

The strongest defensible evidence remains:

- direct misleading or unsupported public claims;
- the TSE finding concerning use of presidential resources;
- mixed evidence distinguishing Bolsonaro personally from allegations involving relatives and associates.

Personal enrichment, procurement benefit, asset-disclosure violations, and settled target-period corruption findings remain unresolved.

### Chapter 8B — Effectiveness/competence

New evidence:

- `WEB061`: TCU reported that Auxílio Brasil reached 21.6 million families in all 5,570 municipalities with a R$13 billion investment at the time of the December 2022 report. This supports implementation scale and national program reach, while not establishing durability or quality. [Brazilian government/TCU program report](https://www.gov.br/pt-br/noticias/assistencia-social/2022/12/tcu-define-auxilio-brasil-como-o-programa-de-transferencia-de-renda-mais-efetivo-na-reducao-da-pobreza/c0c12b92-5a30-4357-bdda-3e54bba2b0a5.jpeg/view), lines 108–115.  
  Mappings: `8B.2, 8B.6, 8B.7, 8B.10`

The TCU audit in `WEB056` provides contrary implementation evidence: large reach coexisted with targeting errors, family fragmentation, and weaker cost-effectiveness. Searches covered coordination, adaptation, correction, appointments, implementation audits, and durability. No comprehensive portfolio evaluation or robust evidence of cross-program adaptation was recovered.

## Rejected/discovery-only items

- `WEB062`: Later police accusations concerning alleged vaccination-record falsification. Retained as retrospective allegation/investigative material, not a settled 2022 finding.  
  Disposition: `rejected_discovery`; mappings: `7B.3, 7B.6, 7B.7, 7B.8`

- `WEB063`: Later TSE proceedings concerning 7 September 2022 and electoral-resource conduct. Search results identified the proceeding, but the accessible record was an intermediate vote rather than a complete final decision.  
  Disposition: `rejected_discovery`; mappings: `4B.1, 4B.2, 4B.8, 4B.10, 7B.6, 7B.7`

- `WEB064`: Search-result reports concerning federal investigations into education and Yanomami administration without a directly opened primary report.  
  Disposition: `rejected_discovery`; mappings: `3B.5, 3B.6, 6B.5, 6B.6, 8B.3, 8B.5`

## Updated continuation assessment

- `1B`: institutional nuclear exposure improved; personal attribution remains very weak.
- `2B`: official diplomatic posture improved; broader security conduct remains incomplete.
- `3B`: Yanomami institutional deterioration is better documented; protest policing, surveillance, and remedies remain weak.
- `4B`: no new final unit; existing contrary election-administration evidence remains important.
- `5B`: TCU added precise fiscal, targeting, cost-effectiveness, and regional-distribution evidence.
- `6B`: education exclusion and learning-recovery implementation gaps are now better documented.
- `7B`: no additional settled personal-integrity evidence; personal-benefit nexus remains unresolved.
- `8B`: program scale and implementation shortcomings are better documented, but adaptation, coordination, and durability remain weak.

The continuation produced a defensible but still uneven handoff. Several chapters remain below ideal breadth, especially 1B, 4B, and 7B. The evidence should be passed to the formatter and chapter judge only with the attribution, retrospective-status, duplication, and contrary-evidence labels preserved.
